result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers find the same core problems: seven competing hues, green links that look like on-time status, orange that reads as a warning, white on amber at about 1.9:1, and the failing muted gray. Both give concrete replacement values while keeping the blue primary and neutral surfaces. A edges ahead because its problems are explicitly ranked by impact with the worst legibility failures first, which a developer can work through in order. B has a clearer contrast table and a fuller status token system, but it leads with the role-overlap problem rather than the most severe failures. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers find the same main problems: too many unrelated hues, a green link that looks like the on-time status, an orange that reads as a warning, white text on yellow, and light gray meta text. Both also give concrete replacement CSS. B wins on organization because it ranks the issues by impact, putting the two worst legibility failures first. B also makes more explicit what it keeps: the blue primary, the familiar status hues and the neutral scheme. A is equally thorough but leads with the palette theory and moves the status colors to tinted fills.
